blocks.text: Compounds in which a hydroxyl group is bonded to an aromatic ring (an arene) are phenols. The simplest is phenol itself, C6H5OH, also known as carbolic acid, once used in carbolic soap; it is a white crystalline solid. Other examples are 1-naphthol and 2-naphthol, with the -OH group on naphthalene.
Phenol can be made from phenylamine and nitrous acid (HNO2) in three steps:

items: Nitrous acid is too unstable to store, so it is made in the test tube from sodium nitrite (NaNO2) and dilute hydrochloric acid, kept below 10 C with ice.
Phenylamine reacts with the nitrous acid to form an unstable diazonium salt, benzenediazonium chloride, C6H5N2+ Cl-.
On warming, the diazonium salt is hydrolysed (decomposed) by water, giving phenol and nitrogen gas: C6H5N2+ Cl- + H2O -> C6H5OH + N2 + HCl.

blocks.alt: Top: phenol, 2-naphthol and 1-naphthol. Bottom: phenylamine with NaNO2 + HCl below 10 C gives benzenediazonium chloride, which on warming with water gives phenol + N2 + HCl.
blocks.caption: Phenolic compounds and the preparation of phenol (original diagram after the book's structures and scheme).
blocks.long_description: A phenol has the -OH group joined directly to an aromatic ring. To make phenol, the -NH2 group of phenylamine is first turned into a diazonium group, -N2+, in the cold; on warming, the diazonium group leaves as nitrogen gas and is replaced by -OH from water.
